title: Comparing and choosing
job: More, less, better — stating a preference
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: A + es + más/menos + Adj + que + B

rules.text: The comparative is two words around an unchanged adjective: más caro que, menos caro que. English forks between -er and "more" and Spanish never does — the adjective itself does not move.
The superlative adds the article to the same frame: el más caro, la más barata. Nothing else changes.
mejor and peor replace más bueno and más malo, and mejor serves bien as well — canta mejor is "sings better". "mejor is the comparative of bueno" is only half of it.
este and esta point at what is here and agree with the noun: este libro, esta tienda, estas manzanas. They are not L1-M1's ésta-less está — the accent and the position keep them apart.
cuál asks you to pick from a set that both speakers know about: ¿Cuál prefieres? qué asks openly. English uses "which" and "what" the same way.

words.note: Points at what is near, and agrees with the noun: este libro, esta tienda. Nothing about it is like L1-M1's esto.
Goes in front of the adjective and leaves it alone: más caro, más grande, más difícil. It carries an accent, which separates it from mas, an old word for "but" nobody says.

sentences.trap: The adjective does not change at all. English has caro → more expensive AND grande → bigger; Spanish has one shape for both.
sentences.sound: MAS, one syllable, and the accent marks meaning rather than stress.

variations.changed: feminine, and both words follow it
a two-cell adjective, and más still does the work
plural throughout

mistake.why: caro with one r is expensive; carro with two is a cart or a car. The r is the whole difference.

sentences.usage: The everyday comparison, with the second thing left unsaid because it is obvious.
sentences.mnemonic: más goes in front and the adjective never moves.

sentences.display: El metro es más rápido que el autobús.
sentences.cue: The metro is faster than the bus.
sentences.literal: The metro is more fast than the bus.

words.note: Four shapes. The accent marks a stress two syllables from the end, as in teléfono and número.

sentences.trap: que here is not M5's "that" and not M4's qué. Same spelling, and the sentence decides which job it is doing.
sentences.sound: RA-pi-do, stressed on the first syllable, with the initial r rolled.

variations.display: El autobús es menos rápido que el metro.
variations.cue: The bus is less fast than the metro.
variations.changed: the comparison turned round with menos
the second thing left unsaid
muy instead of más — no comparison at all

mistake.display: El metro es más rápido de el autobús.
mistake.why: The word for "than" is que. de appears in a superlative — el más rápido de la ciudad — and nowhere else here.

sentences.usage: Comparing two named things. The que is what makes the second one appear.
sentences.mnemonic: más … que, and nothing between them changes.

words.note: The feminine of este, and it is NOT M2's está — that one has an accent and is a verb. Esta tienda está cerca has both in one sentence. The row for este is S01's.
The mirror of más, and it works exactly the same way: menos caro, menos rápido. It ends in -s in the singular and never changes.

sentences.trap: esta and está are one accent apart and sit in the same sentence shapes. Dropping it turns a pointing word into a verb.
sentences.sound: ME-nos, and the two words of esta and está are told apart only by where the stress falls.

variations.changed: masculine, and both words move
esta and está in one sentence, doing different jobs

variations.display: Es menos caro que el otro.
variations.cue: It's less expensive than the other one.
variations.changed: M5's otro standing alone as "the other one"

mistake.why: The pointing word carries no accent: esta tienda. With one it is the verb.

sentences.usage: Softer than saying something is cheap, which is why shops use it and customers do not.
sentences.mnemonic: No accent points; an accent is a verb.

sentences.display: Es la tienda más barata de la calle.
sentences.cue: It's the cheapest shop in the street.
sentences.literal: Is the shop most cheap of the street.

words.note: Four shapes, and the everyday opposite of caro. It carries none of the English suggestion that a cheap thing is a poor one.

sentences.trap: The group takes de, not en: la más barata DE la calle. English says "in" and Spanish says "of".
sentences.sound: ba-RA-ta, with a single tapped r in the middle.

variations.changed: masculine, and the group left unsaid

variations.display: Es la tienda más cara de la calle.
variations.cue: It's the most expensive shop in the street.
variations.changed: the opposite superlative
plural, and everything agrees with it

mistake.display: Es la tienda más barata en la calle.
mistake.why: A superlative marks its group with de: la más barata de la calle.

sentences.usage: How a shop is recommended. The de-phrase is what makes it a claim rather than an opinion.
sentences.mnemonic: The best OF a group, never IN it.

words.note: Replaces más bueno, which nobody says, and it also serves bien: habla mejor is "speaks better". One word where English has two.

sentences.trap: No más in front of it. mejor already carries the comparison, exactly as English's "better" does.
sentences.sound: me-HOR, stressed at the end, with the j a breathy h.

variations.display: Este café es mejor que el otro.
variations.cue: This coffee is better than the other one.
variations.changed: the second thing named with que

variations.display: Es el mejor café de la calle.
variations.cue: It's the best coffee in the street.
variations.changed: the superlative, which is the same word with an article

variations.display: Esta tienda es mejor que la otra.
variations.cue: This shop is better than the other one.
variations.changed: mejor with the second thing named

mistake.why: mejor is already a comparison. más doubles it, exactly as English's "more better" does.

sentences.usage: The commonest comparison anyone makes, and the one most often said with nothing after it.
sentences.mnemonic: One word for better and for more good.

words.note: The mirror of mejor, replacing más malo and also serving mal. One shape for either gender.

sentences.trap: estar, because today's soup is a state rather than what soup is. es peor would be a claim about soup in general.
sentences.sound: pe-OR, two syllables — the e and the o do not glide together.

variations.display: Este café es peor que el otro.
variations.cue: This coffee is worse than the other one.
variations.changed: ser, because it is a quality and not a state
about a person, and still estar

variations.display: Es la peor tienda de la calle.
variations.cue: It's the worst shop in the street.
variations.changed: the superlative, in front of the noun

mistake.display: La sopa está más mala hoy.
mistake.why: más malo is not what people say: peor. The same rule that gives mejor for bueno.

sentences.usage: A complaint made gently, because it compares rather than accuses.
sentences.mnemonic: peor is to malo what mejor is to bueno.

words.note: The partner of M2's mayor, and it works the same way: one shape, no más in front, and it is about age rather than size.

sentences.trap: menor and mayor rank people; más pequeño and más grande measure them. Spanish keeps the two jobs apart and English does not.
sentences.sound: me-NOR, stressed at the end, exactly like mejor and peor.

variations.display: Mi hermana es menor que mi hermano.
variations.cue: My sister is younger than my brother.
variations.changed: the comparison completed with que

variations.display: Mi hermano menor es muy alto.
variations.cue: My younger brother is very tall.
variations.changed: menor after the noun, saying which brother
plural, which adds -es

mistake.why: menor already compares. más doubles it, as it would with mejor.

sentences.usage: Family talk. mayor and menor are how siblings are ranked, and the ages themselves often never come up.
sentences.mnemonic: mayor and menor rank; grande and pequeño measure.

sentences.display: ¿Cuál prefieres, la sopa o el pan?
sentences.cue: Which do you prefer, the soup or the bread?
sentences.literal: Which prefer(you), the soup or the bread?

words.note: Picks from a set both speakers know about. qué asks openly — ¿Qué quieres? — and the two are not interchangeable.
preferir, with the e→ie change M1 named: prefiero, prefieres, prefiere, but preferir. The third time this course has met that pattern.

sentences.trap: cuál carries an accent because it asks. The unaccented cual joins clauses and does not appear in this course.
sentences.sound: KWAL, one syllable. pre-FYE-res, stressed on the ie.

variations.changed: the set left unsaid because it is in front of you
cuál with the comparison instead of the verb
the plural, when the set has more than two

mistake.display: ¿Qué prefieres, la sopa o el pan?
mistake.why: With the choice named in front of you it is cuál. qué would be asking what kind of thing you like.

sentences.usage: A waiter, a shopkeeper, a friend at a table. The or-list is what makes cuál the right word.
sentences.mnemonic: cuál picks from a set; qué asks into the air.

sentences.cue: I prefer the fish, it's better.

words.note: The I-form, with the ie the whole verb takes when the stress lands on it. The row for preferir is S08's.

sentences.trap: The second clause has no subject at all. Once the fish has been named, Spanish stops naming it.
sentences.sound: pre-FYE-ro, and the stress moving to the ending in preferir is what flattens it back to an e.

variations.changed: the reason left off

variations.display: Prefiero el café, es más barato.
variations.cue: I prefer the coffee, it's cheaper.
variations.changed: a different reason, using más

variations.display: No prefiero nada, me gusta todo.
variations.cue: I don't prefer anything, I like it all.
variations.changed: the refusal to choose

mistake.why: The stem takes ie when the stress falls on it: prefiero.

sentences.usage: Answering a choice. Naming the reason is what turns a preference into a recommendation.
sentences.mnemonic: Stress the stem and the e breaks into ie.

sentences.display: Estas manzanas son las más baratas.
sentences.literal: These apples are the most cheap.

words.note: The feminine plural of este. The row is S01's, and this is the cell a market sentence needs most.

sentences.trap: The article in las más baratas is not the one in front of manzanas. A superlative always carries its own, even when the noun already had one.
sentences.sound: ES-tas, stressed on the first syllable, which is what keeps it clear of está.

variations.display: Estos libros son los más caros.
variations.cue: These books are the most expensive.
variations.changed: masculine plural throughout
mejor in the plural, which adds -es
the noun dropped once everyone can see it

mistake.display: Estas manzanas son más baratas de todas.
mistake.why: A superlative needs its article: las más baratas de todas.

sentences.usage: A market. Pointing and comparing in one sentence is most of what happens at a stall.
sentences.mnemonic: The superlative brings its own article.
